Okay, let me try to clear this up a bit. Tankless electric water heaters are viable in some cases, and not others. You are going to have to do the math yourself to know if one will work in your situation.

Tankless systems are generally more energy efficient, because they only heat the water you need, as you need it, as opposed to a tank system that has to heat the tanked water to the set point, and then continuously keep it there. The drawback to tankless systems is, there is no tank, no reserve, no buffer, it can't give you 50 gallons of hot water instantly. I hope I can explain this.

Tankless water heaters are rated by how many gallons per minute of water they can heat by a certain temperature rise. The one you linked will heat 7 gallons of water per minute, by 35 degrees Fahrenheit. So if the water entering it (your cold water) is 60 degrees, it will give you 7 gallons at 95 degrees in one minute. So if you want that water to be 140 degrees, you have to restrict the water flow down from 7 GPM so it passes through the heater slower and has a chance to absorb more heat. There should be a curve graph that would show the temperature rise vs. the flow rate, you may have to search the manufactures website for that information. My guess is you may get 2 GPM at 140, but you would have to check the graph. So, if you have a low flow shower head, 1.5 GPM or so, you can probably take a 140 degree shower, but if you just open the tub spigot full tilt, that water isn't going to come out at 140.

So, here's where you need to do the math. What is the maximum water flow in GPM you need and at what temp? How many showers/baths are going to be running at the same time? Will you be doing laundry at the same time? Etc... Then you need to know how much hotter you need to make the water at that GPM flow. So if your cold water is 60, and you want 140, you need to heat that water 80 degrees at that same flow rate. Then you can look for a heater that will do the job.

Once you find one that will work, then look at the electrical requirements. The one you linked is a 36kw unit, it will pull 150 Amps at 240v. This is most likely more power than you even have available at the service coming into your house. No to mention the breaker space it would require.

TL;DR

You could probably get away with a tankless system to replace the water heater that supplies the master bath only, but need to stick with a tank for the second heater that does the rest of the house.
